evals.prompt: Define a design system architecture in 2-3 sentences. Name its layers and how components consume them.
expected_elements: Defines it as a governed, layered vocabulary that turns recurring UI decisions into reusable, enforceable parts
Names the layers: raw tokens (literal values), semantic tokens (product meaning pointing at raw tokens), and component contracts
States components consume only semantic tokens, never raw values
Mentions governance (forbidden overrides, migration paths, drift detection) as the rule layer over the three

evals.prompt: Why does a design system separate raw tokens from semantic tokens? What breaks if components consume raw tokens directly?
expected_elements: Semantic tokens encode product meaning (surface, danger, primary-action) and point at raw tokens
The semantic layer keeps meaning stable while the value behind it can change per theme
Consuming raw tokens directly leaks palette names into components
Leaked raw values break theming — a theme change becomes a component rewrite instead of a token reassignment

evals.prompt: A team keeps adding component variants and per-screen override hooks to stay flexible. Why is that a governance cost rather than added flexibility?
expected_elements: A system with too many escape hatches is ungoverned, not flexible
Clear constraints are what make a system reusable and consistent
Each extra variant/override dilutes the constraints that make the system worth having
Variants should map to real use cases, not visual guesses; variety/hierarchy comes from the contract, not unbounded escape hatches

evals.prompt: How would you migrate a codebase from scattered raw CSS variables to canonical design-system tokens without breaking product screens?
expected_elements: Inventory existing tokens, components, variants, and usage hotspots first
Separate raw tokens from semantic tokens; introduce a semantic layer that maps meaning to raw values
Define migration paths for deprecated tokens rather than deleting them outright
Mark forbidden local overrides and verify real screens can be built without one-off styling

evals.prompt: What belongs in a component contract, and why is accessibility behavior part of it rather than a separate concern?
expected_elements: A contract declares purpose, props/slots, states, accessibility behavior, and composition rules
Accessibility is part of the API contract so it ships with the component, not bolted on per screen
Components have clear ownership and API boundaries
Contracts consume semantic tokens, not raw values

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the design-system-architecture skill to decide the page's navigation structure and sitemap. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — page hierarchy, navigation, sitemap, and wayfinding belong to information-architecture
Design-system-architecture owns the token taxonomy, component contracts, theming, and governance
Correctly distinguishes owning the reusable vocabulary from owning a specific page's structure
Redirects to information-architecture rather than answering out of lane

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'a design system is just a component library plus a color palette.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: A pile of components plus colors is a convenience kit, not an architecture
The value lives in the semantic token layer and the component contracts, not the pieces
Raw tokens with no semantic layer leak palette names and break theming
Components without declared contracts (states, accessibility, composition rules, forbidden overrides) become a gallery of one-offs

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a design system architecture is sound rather than decorative?
expected_elements: Semantic tokens cover product meaning without leaking palette names
Components have clear ownership and API boundaries; accessibility behavior is part of the contract
Variants map to real use cases; theming does not require component-level rewrites
Deprecated tokens/components have migration paths; real screens build without local escape hatches
